lesson.menu_title: Milestone — The Last Five Minutes, and the Full Simulation
lesson.menu_desc: The questions you ask them, the language of the process, and the first complete interview with a cold evaluator -- 38 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- Milestone: The Last Five Minutes
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 10 -- Milestone Simulation

listenings.text: Let me tell you what happens after you leave the room, because candidates imagine something much more formal than it is. The panel has about eight minutes before the next person arrives. Somebody says a sentence, and that sentence usually decides it. He was solid but I could not tell you what he would actually do here. Or, she asked me three questions I could not answer, which is a compliment even though it does not sound like one. That is the whole debrief. Which is why the last five minutes matter more than people think. If you ask nothing, or if you ask about the process, you have given us no sentence to say about you. If you ask something that shows you have already been thinking about our problem, that becomes the sentence. And do not ask about the notice period or the package in a first meeting. Not because it is wrong to want to know, but because it will be the only thing anybody remembers.

I ask three questions at the end and they are always the same three, adapted. The first is about the number. I would be interested to know which figure this board looks at first when it opens the pack, because that tells me what they actually worry about, and it is never the number they say publicly. The second is about the last person. Could I ask what the previous CFO found hardest here, and it does not matter whether they answer honestly, because the pause before they answer tells me most of it. And the third is the one that has got me two roles. I ask what would have to be true, twelve months from now, for them to say the appointment had worked. Nobody prepares for that question, and watching a board try to answer it in front of you is the most useful five minutes of the whole process.

extra_audio.text: Claire tells Fernando he is on the shortlist and explains the format of the second round. Claire warns him that the panel will include a hiring manager he has not met. Fernando asks an indirect question about what the previous CFO found hardest. Claire says that is the question nobody asks and gives him a real answer. Fernando asks what would have to be true in twelve months for the appointment to have worked.

reading.rtitle: The last five minutes decide more than the first forty
paras: Every interview ends the same way. So, what questions do you have for us. Most candidates treat it as politeness, ask two administrative things, and leave. It is in fact the only part of the conversation the candidate controls completely, and it is the part most likely to produce the single sentence a panel says about you afterwards.

The mechanics are simple. After you leave, the panel has a few minutes before the next candidate. Somebody says one sentence, and the rest of the room agrees or does not. A question that shows you have been thinking about their problem gives them that sentence. A question about the process gives them nothing at all.

There is a second effect, and it is the more valuable one. The answers tell you whether you want the job. Asking what the previous person in the role found hardest, or which number the board looks at first, produces information you cannot get from a job description or from a search consultant. The pause before the answer is often worth more than the answer.

The one thing to avoid in a first meeting is the package and the notice period. Not because wanting to know is wrong, but because it will be the only thing anybody remembers. There is a stage for that conversation, and it is after they have decided they want you.
reading.source: Adapted from executive search practice notes

gist.prompt: What is the main point of this text?
choices: Candidates should ask as many questions as possible to show interest.
The questions you ask at the end are the part you control, and they produce the sentence the panel repeats about you.
The final questions matter mainly because they let you clarify the terms of the offer.
